Consult Summary:
- 32-year-old postpartum woman (C-section 4 weeks ago) with acute-onset shortness of breath for ~1 hour, new cough since yesterday, and subjective tachycardia; clinician concerned for possible pulmonary embolism and advised urgent hospital evaluation.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Acute shortness of breath beginning while sitting watching TV, onset approximately 1 hour prior to the call.
  - New cough started yesterday; no sputum production reported.
  - Subjective awareness of a fast heart rate/palpitations.
  - Chest soreness on deep inspiration; patient attributes some chest tenderness to recent C‑section scar.
- Timeline/progression:
  - Cough started yesterday.
  - Shortness of breath developed acutely over the hour before the consult.
  - Took codeine fairly regularly after C‑section; stopped taking it about 1 week ago.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Occurred at rest; no specific exacerbating or relieving factors reported.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems (as reported):
  - No haemoptysis reported.
  - No reported leg pain or swelling.
  - No fever, chills, or other infective symptoms documented.
  - Patient reports feeling “stressed”/anxious about her heart racing.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No prior episodes of similar shortness of breath.
  - No other chronic medical problems reported by patient.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.
- Obstetric history:
  - Recent cesarean section 4 weeks ago.
- Medications:
  - Codeine — taken “fairly regularly” post‑C‑section; stopped ~1 week ago (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Allergies:
  - Ibuprofen — reaction not specified.

Social History:
- Lives with partner (partner was at work at time of call).
- Newborn baby present at home and with patient during call.
- No tobacco, alcohol, or substance use documented in transcript.

Family History:
- Mother has had clots in her legs (family history of venous thromboembolism).

Physical Examination:
- Vitals:
  - No formal vital signs (BP, RR, SpO2, temperature) documented.
  - Pulse palpation: patient counted "30" beats during the clinician’s timed count; clinician documented this as “slightly fast” (palpation-based assessment only).
- Other exam findings:
  - No additional physical exam findings documented.

Investigations:
- No investigations, imaging, or laboratory results reported in the transcript.

Assessment & Plan:
- Integrate transcript impressions with DDx priorities: primary clinical concern is acute venous thromboembolism (pulmonary embolism) given recent C‑section, acute dyspnea, tachycardia, and family history of clots. Other plausible considerations include acute respiratory infection and peripartum cardiomyopathy. Immediate plan from clinician: urgent hospital assessment.

- Issue 1: Possible pulmonary embolism (PE)
  - Assessment:
    - Acute-onset dyspnea at rest 4 weeks postpartum after C‑section; subjective tachycardia on palpation; family history of VTE — clinician explicitly concerned for clot and advised urgent evaluation.
  - Plan (per transcript / clinician advice):
    - Patient instructed to go to the hospital promptly for further assessment.
    - Patient advised not to take codeine for the time being prior to evaluation.
    - If PE is confirmed in hospital, anticoagulation may be initiated (clinician stated hospital can give “something to reduce the clot”).
    - Transport options discussed: ambulance offered; patient elected to self-transport with baby and belongings.
    - Hospital will determine specific diagnostic testing and treatment per local protocols.

- Issue 2: Acute respiratory infection (bronchitis/pneumonia)
  - Assessment:
    - New cough starting yesterday could reflect viral or bacterial lower respiratory infection contributing to dyspnea.
  - Plan:
    - Included in reason for hospital evaluation; ED assessment may include clinical exam, chest imaging and tests to evaluate for infection as indicated.
    - Manage/support per hospital findings (antibiotics or supportive care if indicated).

- Issue 3: Postpartum cardiac causes (peripartum cardiomyopathy and other cardiac etiologies)
  - Assessment:
    - Timing (4 weeks postpartum) and palpitations raise possibility of peripartum cardiomyopathy or other cardiac cause of dyspnea/tachycardia.
  - Plan:
    - Cardiac evaluation recommended as part of hospital assessment (ECG, clinical assessment; echocardiography if indicated) per ED/cardiology judgment.

- Additional/ancillary considerations discussed or supported by transcript/DDx:
  - Consider postpartum anemia as a potential contributor (history of recent surgery) — hospital may assess hemoglobin.
  - Anxiety/panic may be contributing to symptom perception; should be considered after organic causes are evaluated/excluded.
  - Patient to bring baby and necessary items to hospital; partner not present at home.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Pulmonary embolism (PE)
  - Likelihood: High
  - Rationale: Recent C‑section (4 weeks postpartum) → increased VTE risk; sudden-onset dyspnea and clinician-documented tachycardia; family history of clots. Clinician advised urgent hospital assessment for this reason.
- Acute respiratory infection (pneumonia/bronchitis, including viral)
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: New cough since yesterday could indicate an infectious cause for dyspnea; however abrupt severe dyspnea at rest is somewhat less typical and PE must be excluded first.
- Peripartum (postpartum) cardiomyopathy
  - Likelihood: Moderate
  - Rationale: Occurs in late pregnancy/postpartum window; patient is 4 weeks post‑C‑section with new dyspnea and palpitations — warrants consideration and cardiac evaluation.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective vital signs (heart rate in beats per minute, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature).
  - Length of time over which the pulse count of "30" was measured (timing interval not documented).
  - Details of codeine use (dose, route, frequency) and exact nature of ibuprofen allergy reaction.
  - Any focused cardiopulmonary physical exam (lung auscultation, leg exam for DVT).
  - Laboratory results (CBC, D-dimer, troponin) and imaging (CXR, echocardiogram, CT pulmonary angiography/VQ) — none available.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None identified. (DDx interpretations are consistent with transcript; clinician interpretation of palpated pulse as “slightly fast” aligns with the patient’s counted "30" but the DDx’s bpm conversion was an inference — no direct BPM values were created in this note.)
- Comment on transcript quality:
  - Transcript was audible and clear; relevant history and clinician recommendations were documented.
